content.text: The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of the body. Key cellular components include: The Plasma Membrane (phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins), Nucleus (contains DNA, controls cell activities), Cytoplasm (cytosol + organelles), Mitochondria (ATP production, powerhouses), Endoplasmic Reticulum (protein and lipid synthesis), Golgi Apparatus (protein modification and packaging), Lysosomes (digestion and waste removal), Ribosomes (protein synthesis), and the Cytoskeleton (maintains cell shape and provides movement).

content.text: The plasma membrane is a selective barrier composed of phospholipids, cholesterol, and proteins. The phospholipid bilayer has hydrophilic heads facing outward and hydrophobic tails facing inward. Membrane proteins include: Integral proteins (span the membrane, function as channels, carriers, or receptors) and Peripheral proteins (associated with membrane surface, function in signaling or support). Cholesterol stabilizes the membrane and regulates fluidity. Membrane carbohydrates are involved in cell recognition and adhesion.

content.text: Substances cross the membrane through various mechanisms: Passive Transport (no energy required) includes Simple Diffusion (movement down concentration gradient), Facilitated Diffusion (via carrier proteins), and Osmosis (water movement through aquaporins). Active Transport (requires ATP) includes Primary Active Transport (direct ATP use, e.g., Na+/K+ pump), and Secondary Active Transport (uses electrochemical gradient, e.g., glucose transport). Vesicular Transport includes Endocytosis (phagocytosis, pinocytosis) and Exocytosis (release of molecules).

content.text: The Na+/K+ ATPase pump is essential for maintaining cellular ion gradients. It pumps 3 Na+ out of the cell and 2 K+ into the cell for each ATP hydrolyzed. This maintains a high K+ and low Na+ inside the cell, which is crucial for establishing the resting membrane potential. The pump also drives secondary active transport of glucose and amino acids. Ouabain, a cardiac glycoside, inhibits the Na+/K+ pump, increasing intracellular Na+ and Ca2+, which enhances cardiac contractility.

content.text: All cells maintain a resting membrane potential (RMP), typically -70 mV in neurons. The RMP results from: Unequal distribution of ions (K+ concentrated inside, Na+ outside), Selective permeability of the membrane (more permeable to K+ than Na+), and the activity of the Na+/K+ pump. The Nernst equation calculates the equilibrium potential for a single ion. The Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation accounts for multiple ions. Changes in membrane potential underlie all electrical signaling in excitable tissues.
